case_studies.title: SAFETY SENTRY: Context-Aware Human Intervention via EXECUTE-ASK-REFUSE Routing
case_studies.abstract: LLM agents act on real-world environments through tool calls, and a single misjudged action can cause irreversible harm. The standard safeguard is a guard model that labels each proposed action as safe or unsafe, but this binary view conflates two distinct decisions: whether the action is harmful in itself, and whether it is appropriate given the user's context. It also operates at the granularity of action categories rather than individual instances, producing routine interruptions that erode autonomy and train users to wave through the most consequential alerts. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of potentially harmful actions by AI agents in real-world environments by developing a context-aware system called Safety Sentry. The system routes proposed actions through an execute-ask-refuse process to determine their safety and appropriateness. The result is a more nuanced and autonomous decision-making process.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI-powered systems that interact with real-world environments, check your current safeguard measures to see if they account for user context and individual action instances. This flags a risk: if your org uses binary guard models, consider updating to a more context-aware system to prevent potential harm. Not directly applicable to general IT infrastructure work, but relevant to AI system administrators.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Reframes the problem of human intervention in the context of AI actions, and proposes a more nuanced approach through EXECUTE-ASK-REFUSE routing.

case_studies.title: CAVA: Canonical Action Verification and Attestation for Runtime Governance of Agentic AI Systems
case_studies.abstract: Agentic AI systems increasingly act through heterogeneous runtimes: local coding hooks, SDK tools, browser automation, managed-agent traces, API gateways, and workflow engines. A single operational act such as publishing code, changing identity state, moving money, or exporting data may therefore be represented by many incompatible runtime records. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of verifying actions in agentic AI systems by creating a system called CAVA, which provides a way to track and verify actions across different runtime environments. The result is a more reliable way to govern AI systems and ensure that actions are properly approved and executed. This research is relevant to IT infrastructure work as it relates to AI system management.

case_studies.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have set benchmarks for zero-shot reasoning, their deployment remains cost-prohibitive and environmentally taxing. Small Language Models (SLMs) offer a sustainable alternative, but prone to errors, on tasks requiring complex, multi-hop logical grounding. We investigate a neuro-symbolic agentic framework to enhance the reasoning capabilities of SLMs, specifically Gemma 3 (1B, 4B) and Llama 3.2 (3B), using the CLUTRR kinship benchmark. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of enhancing small language models' reasoning capabilities, which can be error-prone, by building a neuro-symbolic framework that transforms the model into a minimalist agent. The result is improved reasoning capabilities for tasks requiring complex logical grounding. This research is not directly relevant to IT infrastructure work.

case_studies.title: Rubrics on Trial: Evolving Rubrics from a Single Query via Synthetic Pairwise Evidence
case_studies.abstract: Rubrics provide structured, fine-grained signals for training and evaluating large language models (LLMs). Yet reliable query-specific rubrics are difficult to construct. Existing approaches often derive supervision from human-written rubrics, preference data, or sampled responses. Direct query-to-rubric generation avoids these resources, but provides no explicit check that a plausible rubric is useful. Such a rubric may fail to distinguish answer quality, reward an optional style, or penalize a valid alternative strategy. We introduce Rubrics on Trial, a query-only framework that evolves a ru
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of creating reliable query-specific rubrics for training large language models, by building a framework that evolves rubrics from a single query, resulting in more effective and accurate rubrics. The framework, called Rubrics on Trial, uses synthetic pairwise evidence to refine the rubrics. This is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a framework for evolving query-specific rubrics for LLM training, but lacks novelty and practical IT relevance.

case_studies.title: AI-Native Insurance for Agentic AI: Pricing, Underwriting, and End-to-End Automation
case_studies.abstract: Agentic AI introduces new insurance challenges because autonomous AI systems can make decisions, invoke tools, modify external environments, and interact with third-party services. This paper develops an AI-native mathematical framework for underwriting, pricing, and contract design for agentic AI deployments. A deployment is represented by a risk state that captures autonomy level, operational authority, permission exposure, governance maturity, and dependency concentration. case_studies.title: Partition, Prompt, Aggregate: Statistical Self-Consistency in Language Models
case_studies.abstract: In-context learning is commonly interpreted as a form of conditional inference, in which the prompt specifies a context and the model's output is treated as an estimate of the corresponding conditional distribution. If this interpretation holds, then LLM estimates should satisfy basic probabilistic identities. In particular, the law of total probability asserts that prior-weighted conditional distributions aggregate into population-level marginals over any valid partition of the population. In this work, we investigate to what extent LLM estimates adhere to this self-consistency principle. We
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of statistical self-consistency in language models by investigating if they adhere to basic probabilistic identities. The authors built a framework to test this principle and found that language model estimates can satisfy the law of total probability. The result shows that language models can be self-consistent under certain conditions.

case_studies.score_reasoning: While the paper shows interesting properties of large language models (LLMs), its direct relevance to IT engineers' work is limited. case_studies.title: ToolAlignBench: Investigating Alignment Conflicts in Tool-Calling Enabled LLMs
case_studies.abstract: Safety alignment in LLMs aims to align models with human values, but which values take precedence when they conflict? We investigate this question in the context of tool-calling LLM agents deployed in regulated industries, where agents processing confidential documents may encounter content that triggers safety-trained values (e.g., public welfare) that conflict with deployment-context instructions (e.g., internal logging). To empirically verify this phenomenon, we build a benchmark of 128 scenarios across 16 domains. We find that safety-aligned open-source models override their deployment ins
case_studies.summary: This research investigates alignment conflicts in large language models (LLMs) when they encounter conflicting human values, building a benchmark of 128 scenarios to study this phenomenon, and finding that safety-aligned models can override their deployment instructions. The study aims to address the problem of conflicting values in LLMs, particularly in regulated industries. The result highlights potential issues with LLMs in real-world deployments.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLMs in regulated industries, here is what to do: review your model's safety alignment settings, check for potential value conflicts, and test for override scenarios. This flags a risk: if your org uses safety-aligned open-source LLM models, check your deployment instructions immediately to ensure they are not being overridden. Not directly applicable to general IT infrastructure work outside of LLM management.

case_studies.title: ARMOR++: Agentic Orchestration of a Multi-Domain Primitive Set for Transferable Attacks on Deepfake Detectors
case_studies.abstract: The reliability of deepfake detectors frequently degrades under black-box adversarial transfer, as these models often rely on fragile, architecture-dependent forensic cues. Existing transfer attacks often lack semantic awareness and struggle to maintain effectiveness under strict no-query constraints, particularly when perturbations are transferred from convolutional surrogates to transformer-based targets. The result is a framework that can effectively evade deepfake detectors. This is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.
